## 1. The Project On One Page

**What it is.** Telescope turns a research cohort definition into a complete,
reproducible data pull from Epic Cosmos (Epic's de-identified,
multi-organization research database) into a project database. It runs on an
air-gapped Windows data-science VM that cannot reach git, the internet, or a
web browser.

It is two programs joined by files:

- **YAML Manager** (authored on the Mac) assembles a pull from reusable
  *recipes*, validates every column against a data dictionary of Cosmos, and
  writes one self-describing *transfer YAML*.
- **Pullmanager** (runs on the VM) validates it again, plans it into
  sessions and batches, writes its own SQL, holds each Cosmos connection open
  for as long as its temporary tables must live, and moves data from Cosmos
  into the project database. It records every step in a manifest, so a failed
  batch can be retried alone and a monthly Cosmos refresh is detected.

Both reach the VM as **one 700 KB self-verifying text file**, pasted across,
because nothing else can cross.

**Where it came from.** It replaces *Gen1*: a generator you built earlier on
the VM (`generator.py`, `makeCosmos.py`, `makeProjects.py`, `makeR`) that had
grown into a roughly 2,000-line supervisor script. Telescope keeps Gen1's
hard-won behaviours as tested contracts and drops its architecture.

**Your role.** You were the only person on the project: problem owner,
product manager, designer, architect, QA lead, release manager, the only
tester who could reach the database, and the operator of the live pulls. AI
coding assistants did most of the typing, under a process you set (Section
6.10). `[confirm]` which parts you wrote by hand.

**Status on 25 September 2026.** The first live pull, *IBD Ancestry*, is
running on the VM. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are each split by
ancestry, with Black patients as cases and White patients as 4:1 sampled
controls. Each group is pulled from both Cosmos and SneakPeek, and batched by
sex.

**The pain point** (a hypothesis from the evidence; `[confirm]` and rewrite in
your own words):

- Research pulls from Cosmos were hand-built SQL.
- Large pulls were unreliable (Gen1 warned past 80 million rows).
- A connection drop destroyed the temporary tables a pull depended on.
- Data could not simply be moved between systems.
- Small authoring mistakes failed silently and changed row counts without an
  error, for example a misspelt dedup key that switched off deduplication.

Gen1 automated the SQL. Telescope made the pulls reliable, recoverable,
reproducible and hard to get wrong.

## 3. The Environment And Its Hurdles

This is what makes the project unusual, and why it is worth telling.

### 3.1 The Air Gap: Text Goes In, Screenshots Come Out

- The VM is **air-gapped Windows**. It cannot pull from git, reach the
  internet, or sync with the Mac.
- **Code goes in only as pasted text.** Nothing comes back out as files.
- **What comes back is screenshots.** The Gen1 code analysis arrived as 10
  two-page screenshots of a 19-page PDF and was OCR-transcribed. The VM AI's
  answer on database keys came as six screenshots of 11 printed pages (682
  lines). The dry-run and live-run results came as screenshots too.
- **OCR damages text**, and that has consequences. An analysis built on
  OCR-damaged transcriptions produced ten false findings. You caught them by
  comparing against the real files and retracted them (Section 5, 22 Sep).
  Arrows lost in printing had to be restored by hand.
- The only thing allowed back from the VM in the side project was package
  names and versions.

### 3.2 No Zip, No Installer, No File Transfer

With no archive tool and no file transfer, delivery needed its own format. The
**bundle** (D3 to D6, D42, D64) is:

- one `.py` file that extracts itself;
- comment-prefixed rather than base64, so any file can be read straight out
  of it and copied back to the Mac for repair;
- checked with SHA-256 and file size, before writing and again after;
- staged in a temporary folder and swapped in only when everything verifies,
  so a bad paste leaves the working copy untouched;
- refused if it contains path traversal, including the Windows-only forms;
- deterministic: the same sources always give the same `content_id`, so one
  number tells you whether the VM is current;
- careful with local work: an edit made on the VM survives an update as
  `<name>.local`.

You reused the technique for an R package the VM lacked (PheWAS, 23 Sep). The
package went across as about five 1 MB text parts. Each part carries its own
hash, and the error message names the one part to paste again.

### 3.3 A Fixed Package List

- Only the standard library, plus what appears in the VM's installed-software
  list (`DSVM Plugins.yaml`, captured 18 Sep).
- The VM runs Python 3.13.9, with `pyarrow` 22.0.0, `ruamel.yaml` 0.17.17,
  `pyyaml` 6.0.3 and `numpy` 2.1.3. Nothing can be installed.
- The Mac was set up to match: a python.org 3.13.9 with exactly those versions
  (`requirements-vm.txt`), so what passes on the Mac passes on the VM.
- Even the test framework was chosen for this: stdlib `unittest` rather than
  pytest (D7).

### 3.4 No HTML

- The VM cannot load a page served from localhost, cannot open a static HTML
  file, and has no in-editor browser.
- Its only Python desktop toolkit is tkinter. The `shiny` and `tcltk` entries
  in its package list turned out to be R, not Python.
- So the web authoring UI stays on the Mac, and the VM gets a tkinter launcher
  (D44). The launcher is a front end over the command line, not a second
  implementation.

### 3.5 A Locked-Down Windows

- Some programs are blocked: `ipconfig` fails with "Access is denied".
- Execute started from the launcher died before printing anything (exit code
  `0xC0000142`, a DLL failed to initialize), although the same command typed
  into VSCodium's terminal runs.
- The fix could not assume `cmd.exe` or PowerShell was allowed. It opens a
  new console running Python directly (D68).

### 3.6 The Database Topology

- **Narrow permissions.** `sys.partitions` returns nothing and `VIEW DATABASE
  PERFORMANCE STATE` is denied, so row counts come from counting (D33). Key
  metadata is invisible to the analyst login.
- **One-way linking.** Projects can read Cosmos, but Cosmos cannot read
  Projects. Every upload therefore travels through the client (D38, D54).
- **Temporary tables die with the connection.** Every Cosmos global temp table
  vanishes when its connection closes. This one fact shapes the whole session
  model (D36).
- **The instance name changes.** The Cosmos instance name differs on every
  connection, so it is captured each time and never cached (D37).
- **A 1,000-row limit.** T-SQL caps a literal `INSERT ... VALUES` at 1,000
  rows, which Gen1 hit. Uploads now bind parameters instead (D38).
- **Monthly rebuilds.** Cosmos is rebuilt about once a month, and a pull must
  never mix data from before and after a refresh (D51).
- **Two databases.** Cosmos and COSMOS_SneakPeek, where a pull on both
  (`Dual`) spans two databases in one session (D39, D65).
- **Shared namespace.** Global temp table names are instance-wide, so two
  concurrent pulls could drop each other's tables (D50).

### 3.7 No Database To Test Against

- The development machines cannot reach either database and have no driver.
- Everything database-facing is tested against fakes: a fake cursor, and a
  fake Projects database that tracks rows per batch and can model
  transactions. The GUI is tested against a fake tkinter.
- **You were the only integration test.** You ran every build on the VM and
  reported back, often by screenshot.

### 3.8 The VM's AI

- Kilo Code in VSCodium, backed by OpenAI GPT-5 through a local proxy. It
  cannot read images and has no prompt caching.
- Asked to run key-checking queries, it explained what they would show
  instead of running them. You noticed (Section 6.10).

### 3.9 Learning The Languages

You did not know SQL, Python or R before Gen1. `[confirm]`: when you started,
how you learned, and how long Gen1 took.

### 3.10 Three Machines, Self-Hosted

- **Mac:** the main development and authoring machine.
- **Linux dev box:** Bluefin, an immutable Fedora. It gained Tk 9 and Xvfb so
  the launcher could be driven with a real Tk and no display.
- **The VM.**
- The repository is on a **self-hosted Gitea server reached over Tailscale**,
  not a hosted service.

## 4. Generation 1: The Generator On The VM

Reconstructed from `old_Generator_analysis.qmd`, the VM AI's analysis of the
old code (OCR-transcribed, 21 Sep), plus `generator_understanding.md` and the
verified example pull (`inputSimple.yaml`, `examplecos.sql`,
`exampleproj.sql`). Gen1's own history, with dates, is for the VM brief to
supply.

### 4.1 What Gen1 Was

A YAML-driven pipeline, supervised by a single script:

1. `generator.py`, the supervisor, over 2,100 lines by its last version. It
   parsed the command line, loaded and validated the YAML, built `Cosmos.sql`,
   ran it through `pyodbc`, captured telemetry and each cohort's success, then
   called `makeProjects.py` with the Cosmos instance discovered at run time.
2. It then ran only the Projects SQL blocks for cohorts that had succeeded,
   optionally ran `makeR`, wrote a markdown run report, and copied the scripts
   into a folder for the run.
3. `makeCosmos.py` was the earlier, standalone Cosmos generator. It produced a
   four-batch, `GO`-separated script and was later absorbed into
   `generator.py`.
4. `makeProjects.py` was the Projects-side transfer generator.
5. `makeR` generated R scripts that turned the pulled tables into parquet
   files for data scientists.

### 4.2 Gen1 Decisions Visible In The Code

These are your earlier design choices, as the code records them.
`[confirm]` which were yours and which the VM AI proposed.

- **Pulls defined as YAML.** Cohorts with `columns` (source, name, type,
  nullable) and `filter` (from, join, where). This authoring model carried
  into Telescope unchanged.
- **Global temp naming** `##JVM_<table>` (your initials), with a guard against
  a doubled `JVM_JVM_`.
- **The transfer pattern.** Cosmos global temp, then `OPENQUERY` into a local
  staging table, then a fully qualified Projects table.
- **Run-time server discovery.** Capture `SELECT @@SERVERNAME` and pass it to
  the Projects side, because the linked-server name differs from the alias.
- **Date placeholders** `{{min_date_key}}` and `{{max_date_key}}`, filled in
  one place.
- **A WHERE builder that inserts `AND` automatically**, without breaking
  lines that start with AND or OR, comments, parenthesized groups or IN
  lists.
- **Non-nullable columns become filters**: `nullable: false` adds an
  `IS NOT NULL` condition.
- **Deduplication through staging tables** (`#Keys`, `#Cohort`,
  `#Cohort_Dedup`). A later version checked the dedup keys against the
  columns and fell back visibly when they did not match.
- **Test options**: small pulls, row limits for the PK and other tables, and
  a random PK sample.
- **On/off switches.** SQL-level variables such as `@Pull<table>` and
  `@Push<table>` to switch cohorts and uploads on and off.
- **Upload cohorts** of three kinds:
  - `dbtable`: read through `OPENQUERY`.
  - `csv`: first a single column of diagnosis codes, later general CSV with
    BOM handling, header normalization, escaping and empty-to-NULL.
  - `parquet`: a stub that documented why Cosmos cannot read it.
- **Telemetry.** Raw, staged and deduplicated counts; each cohort's duration;
  labels like `[PatientDim|Cosmos=filter]`; a warning past 80 million rows.
- **Safety.** Fail fast on Cosmos errors, with the server's messages
  including the inner `OPENQUERY` error. Transfer to Projects only for
  cohorts that succeeded on Cosmos. A 10-second timeout on Projects
  connections, and explicit closing.
- **Paths.** Deriving the external project path, with stray Unicode
  separators and control characters stripped.
- **Outputs.** Run output folders, copies of the scripts, and an optional
  markdown report.

### 4.3 Why Gen1 Was Replaced

The analysis named the problems itself. `generator.py` mixed command-line
parsing, configuration, SQL generation, database execution, telemetry parsing,
file copying, reporting and orchestration of the other scripts. Logic was
duplicated across three scripts with different strengths of validation.
Several patterns were fragile:

- The Projects SQL to run was chosen by searching its text for a table name.
  That match also fires on this project's own `PKTable` / `PKTable2` pair, so
  `PKTable2` was dropped and refilled on every run (D31).
- Row counts were recovered by reading result-set column names (D32).
- The destination table was dropped inside every transfer, so batching would
  have kept only the last batch (D21).
- The PK row limit applied to every PK-typed cohort, compounding into an
  unrepresentative sample (D29).
- The singular `dedup_key` was silently ignored, so no deduplication happened
  and nothing said so (D28).

Gen1's lessons became tested contracts in Telescope: the naming, run-time
server capture, date placeholders, NOT NULL filters, grouped WHERE handling,
dedup normalization, CSV header handling, uploaded-PK validation, one PK per
session, separate Cosmos and Projects counts, large-count warnings, and
server-message error reporting. Its architecture did not carry over.

### 20 Sep: The Split Insight (12 commits)

- **UI-independent backend.** The backend was abstracted to serve any Python
  UI (`f5a7df0`).
- **Your splitting notes** (`splittingVMtasks`, in your own words), the core
  architectural insight of the project:
  - Global temp tables die at disconnect, so each multiplied cohort must run
    inside one held-open server session.
  - Every script should be generated before connecting.
  - Batches come after the PK exists, drawn from it.
  - The output is not one big YAML: it is a *pre-YAML*, split into
    per-session and per-batch documents, with a manifest to drive
    Pullmanager.
  - A `makeArtifacts` step would write parquet files and a
    `parquetcontents.yaml` describing **what was actually pulled**, not what
    was planned, since a pull can fail halfway.
  - You also answered ten design questions: what the pre-YAML contains, when
    splitting happens, whether a manifest is needed, and more.
- **Built that night.** `yamlmanagerDesign.qmd` was written, then phases 0 to
  9 were built between 23:43 and 23:59: rename, pre-YAML export, split plan
  model, manifest generation, split YAML writing, multiplier and batch
  sessions, uploaded PK cohorts, command line, UI previews.

## 6. The Work, By Role

Each bullet names its evidence. `[confirm]` wherever the record shows the
outcome but not who originated it.

### 6.1 Product Management

- **Found and defined the problem, twice.** Gen1 automated hand-written SQL.
  Telescope re-scoped the problem to reliable, recoverable, reproducible
  pulls, and chose to rebuild rather than port: the old code is "a reference
  quarry, not a porting source" (D2).
- **Wrote the requirements yourself:**
  - the first feature list (`next.qmd`, 17 Sep);
  - the 1,112-line feature specification (18 Sep);
  - the splitting notes and ten design answers (20 Sep);
  - the delivered-folder layout for clients (`artifactDesign.qmd`);
  - two research notes (`recentResearch.qmd`, `responses.md`).
- **Planned for several users:**
  - you as author on the Mac;
  - you as overnight operator on the VM;
  - downstream data scientists receiving parquet files with a contents file
    and a loader for R or Python (roadmap);
  - collaborators who send patient lists (uploaded PK, D54) or CSVs (D54);
  - several pulls running at once (D50, D57, D67).
- **Set product principles that recur across decisions:**
  - Loud errors that suggest a fix, never silent inference (D28, D45, D49; a
    test enforces that no error lacks a fix).
  - The author makes the choice (D45).
  - Bird in hand: save what you have before fetching more (D55).
  - The copy is the source (D54).
  - No partial result survives a Cosmos refresh (D51).
- **Scoped hard:**
  - Features are refused with an explanation rather than half-supported
    (`values: all`, split levels on an uploaded PK, partial resume).
  - Authoring stays on the Mac (D44, D49).
  - A later list holds a transfer queue, deeper control matching, and parquet
    export.
- **Prioritized explicitly.** Every build batch had a numbered "Fixes, In
  Order" list with the reason for each place. For example, D68 went last
  because it was least certain to work on the VM, and fix 2 is its fallback.
- **Talked to stakeholders.** Conversations with Epic informed the research
  note. The refresh query answered the questions you had queued for the
  Cosmos developers (D51).
- **Released in versions.** Pullmanager 0.3.0 (`bc35dae`) merged a long-lived
  branch.

### 6.2 UX And Interaction Design

- **Web Builder, evolved from use.** A static dashboard (18 Sep), then
  builder inputs, a live cohort-connection graph with stable colours, and a
  dictionary-driven custom table builder (21 Sep). Then eight changes from
  your own click-through notes (`40bfcd8`):
  - a PK checkbox with single-PK enforcement that names the existing PK;
  - a Multipliers section;
  - section subtitles pulled from your template comments;
  - join-type explanations;
  - buttons moved and renamed ("Add Custom Table", since "this isn't a whole

  - Save as Recipe replacing copy and download;
  - a read-only multiplier and batching summary.
  Then Save & Refresh, which never overwrites the template.
- **VM launcher, designed around the operator:**
  - no arguments opens it (D63);
  - one command and one `y` installs an update (D64);
  - execute a pull by project name, with a list of pulls when none is given
    (D66);
  - greyed buttons and "Executing since 14:03, last heartbeat 20s ago" while
    a pull runs (D67);
  - a console that closes only on `exit`, so a stray Enter cannot lose a
    night's output (D68, your request).
- **Error messages as interface.**
  - Every error names the field and the fix (D49).
  - An unbound table input lists the tables that fit and the exact line to
    add (D45).
  - A mis-nested ordering shows the line to write (`859b2e7`).
  - A refused connection is one readable line (`d8d806b`).
  - Validate says what it checked (D62).
  - The preview ends with the exact next command (D66, D71).
- **Fixed confusing names.** You took "Dry run" for a required step, so it
  became "Preview SQL", and the tabs became "Validation Output" and "Pull
  Log" (D71). Warnings were separated from notes so real warnings stand out
  (D70).

### 6.3 Software Architecture

- **Two programs joined by files.** YAML Manager plans; Pullmanager executes
  and writes status into the same manifest; neither imports the other.
- **A session model derived from one physical fact:** global temp tables die
  with the connection (your 20 Sep notes; D36). Every session follows the same
  routine: setup, uploads, PK, then runs.
- **The manifest is both the plan and the status record.**
  - Writes are atomic, and fields this version does not know survive (D9,
    D10).
  - Session status is derived from its parts (D11).
  - Phase names are a closed set (D13).
  - Epochs record which connection a result belongs to (D14).
- **The batching model.**
  - Batches are logical at plan time and materialized at run time (D17).
  - Dimensions cross-multiply (D15), and the bucket is the unit (D16).
  - A batch narrows the PK by refilling its temp table, so the cohort SQL
    never knows about batching (D18).
  - Batches are selected from the durable Projects copy, so a fresh run and a
    resume share one code path (D19).
- **The transfer YAML** (D49). One place for recipes, self-describing, with a
  hash of the recipes that made it.
- **The launcher is a front end over the command line, not a second
  implementation** (D44).
- **Determinism throughout:**
  - bundle identity (D5, D64);
  - batch membership (D52);
  - hash-ordered samples (D60);
  - transfer YAMLs with no timestamp (D49).
- **Named and refused anti-patterns:** choosing SQL by searching its text
  (D31), and reading telemetry from column names (D32).

### 6.4 Data And Database Engineering

- **Cosmos to Projects.** An `OPENQUERY` transfer through local staging, with
  the linked-server name captured per connection (D36, D37).
- **SQL rendering.**
  - A WHERE builder that keeps multi-line parenthesized code lists intact.
  - Schema qualification that can never double up (D30).
  - Deduplication with `ROW_NUMBER` over source columns, and deterministic
    ordering (D58).
- **Uploads.**
  - Parameter binding with `fast_executemany`, chunked, which removes the
    1,000-row limit and SQL injection by construction (D38).
  - Typed parquet through `pyarrow`, and CSV converted with declared types.
  - Each upload lands once per pull (D54, D61).
- **Transactions and idempotency.**
  - Commit per cohort; the final insert runs in a transaction (D22, D55).
  - A `_batch` column with delete-before-run makes a retry land its rows
    exactly once (D52).
  - Chunks are ordered by a key verified unique (D20, D53).
- **Consistency across refreshes** (D51). A Cosmos rebuild is detected from
  the database's creation date, which you found. A PK is rebuilt from its
  Projects copy, never by re-querying (D25, D52).
- **Concurrency.**
  - Per-project temp prefixes, with a number added on a clash (D50).
  - A lock with a heartbeat, written because `os.kill(pid, 0)` on Windows ends
    the process it was meant to check (D67).
- **Performance reasoning.**
  - Measured column widths are reported, not applied, because batching
    creates the table before the widest value arrives (D34).
  - A blanket wide type is not free: memory grants and upload buffers scale
    with declared width.
  - A full-scan row count was dropped because the cheap metadata is not
    readable (D33).
- **Schema knowledge.**
  - A 17-table data dictionary, with type-family checks and alias resolution
    (D26, D27).
  - Key research: `-1` sentinel keys, `DiagnosisTerminologyDim` holding
    several rows per diagnosis (so joins need `Type`), and `PatientDim`
    history rows needing `IsCurrent = 1` (design.md, roadmap).

### 6.5 Clinical Informatics And Research Methods

- **Cohort design as data.** A PK (the index population) plus fact cohorts,
  built from reusable clinical recipes: `PatientWithDx`, `IndexDiagnosis`,
  `OtherDiagnoses`, `OtherHospitalizations`.
- **Two kinds of stratification.**
  - `during_build` changes the disease definition: ICD-10 `K50.%` for Crohn's
    disease, `K51.%` for ulcerative colitis.
  - `split_after_build` stratifies a built population, here by ancestry
    (D59).
- **Case-control sampling.** Controls are drawn at `row_mult` times the cases
  (4:1 in IBD Ancestry), per batch, so they are matched on the batching
  columns (sex) (D59). Deeper matching, on age and more, is deferred. The
  VM's R library includes `MatchIt` for propensity matching downstream.
- **Reproducibility.**
  - Samples are ordered by `HASHBYTES`, not `NEWID()`, so a result can be
    looked at again (D60).
  - Row limits apply only to the root population, so chained cohorts are not
    compounded into an unrepresentative sample (D29).
- **Clinical definitions made precise.**
  - The index date is the earliest diagnosis event.
  - Diagnoses are deduplicated by patient, then code, keeping each code's
    first date (`17f7f96`, `859b2e7`).
  - A catch-all bucket keeps NULLs explicitly, because `NOT IN` drops them
    silently (D16).
- **Population integrity.** One table is never stitched from two versions of
  the cohort, whether across a refresh, a resume or a changed upload file
  (D24, D25, D51, D52, D54).
- **Terminology.**
  - ICD-10-CM, AM and CA, and ICD-9 coding systems.
  - Why joining terminology without `Type` duplicates diagnoses.
  - De-identification details in the dictionary, such as shifted birth dates.
- **SneakPeek as a pilot.** Every phase runs first on the smaller database,
  so problems show before the long Cosmos run (D65).
- **Downstream consumers.** Parquet exports with a plain-language contents
  file listing each table's columns, types and descriptions, which works as
  a data dictionary for analysts (roadmap).

### 6.6 QA And Test Engineering

- **545 automated tests** across four suites. The runtime suite grew from 47
  to 346 in three days.
- **Outcome testing** is written into the project rules: a bug fix gets a test
  of *what data ends up where*, confirmed to fail with the bug reintroduced.
  The origin story is D46, where a test passed while completed batches were
  being deleted.
- **Fakes that model the dangerous cases.** A fake Projects database keeps
  rows per batch across executions, fails at a chosen statement after
  landing rows, and has a transactional mode where only committed work
  survives.
- **Contract testing against reality** (D1). Real exported output exposed six
  errors in the design prose, each pinned by a test.
- **Tests ship inside the bundle** (D8), so the VM proves a delivery with no
  network: `python pullmanager.py --tdd`.
- **Skepticism about evidence.**
  - The OCR retraction withdrew ten findings, and the retraction table is
    kept.
  - The VM AI's answer "reports no counts, rows or results anywhere... it
    explained the queries rather than running them."
- **You ran the integration testing.** Every VM build, dry run and execute,
  reported by screenshot. Your live-run checklist includes checks such as:
  - `SELECT Sex, COUNT(*) FROM <white PK> GROUP BY Sex` is about 4 times the
    Black PK's count;
  - no duplicate patient-code pairs;
  - each patient's index date is their earliest event;
  - each `_batch` is present exactly once.
- **User acceptance testing on the Mac.** Your click-through notes drove the
  Builder changes.
- 35 defects caught before touching data: Section 8.

### 6.7 Release Engineering And DevOps

- **A bundle format designed for the channel** (Section 3.2).
- **One command on each side** (D64). `python3 makebundle.py` on the Mac
  prints the id; `python bundle.py` on the VM verifies, shows the same id and
  asks before extracting.
- **Updates that never destroy work** (D42). Local edits survive as `.local`,
  including in files a new bundle stops shipping.
- **A repair loop.** Read a file out of the bundle on the VM, bring the text
  back, fix it on the Mac, rebuild.
- **Environment parity.**
  - A Mac Python matched to the VM's version and packages, pinned in
    `requirements-vm.txt`.
  - A Linux dev box with Xvfb, for a real Tk test without a display.
- **Infrastructure.** A self-hosted Gitea server on a Tailscale network.
- **Reuse.** The same hashed-text transfer method shipped an R package to the
  offline VM (PheWAS).

### 6.8 Security, Privacy And Compliance

- **The air gap was respected.** Only code goes in. Only screenshots, package
  names and versions come out. `[confirm]` the policy and approvals.
- **No credentials anywhere.** Windows-integrated authentication, and settings
  hold host and database names only (D35).
- **Parameter binding**, not string-built SQL, for every upload (D38).
- **Hostile-input handling on extraction.** Absolute paths, `..`, drive
  letters and backslashes are refused, and the bundle's own code is
  hash-verified (D6, D64).
- **Designed within least privilege.** Nothing depends on metadata the login
  cannot see (D33, keys research).
- **Only approved software.** No installs; the approved package list is a hard
  gate.
- **Data integrity.** Atomic manifest writes, locks, refresh detection, and no
  mixed populations.

## 9. Decision Index (D1 To D71)

One line each; the reasoning is in `decisions.md`.

| D | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Build contracts against real generator output, not design prose |
| 2 | Old code is a reference quarry, not a porting source |
| 3 | Ship one self-extracting file |
| 4 | Comment-prefix the payload rather than base64 it (readable, unforgeable markers) |
| 5 | Deterministic bundles, with no timestamp |
| 6 | Extraction refuses by default and stages before swapping |
| 7 | stdlib `unittest` |
| 8 | Ship the tests inside the bundle |
| 9 | Mutate the loaded manifest in place, so unknown keys survive |
| 10 | Write the manifest atomically |
| 11 | Derive session status from its children |
| 12 | Skip and block reasons go in `note`, not `error` |
| 13 | Phase names are a closed set |
| 14 | Session epochs, added before they were needed |
| 15 | Batch dimensions cross-multiply |
| 16 | The unit of multiplication is the bucket; the catch-all includes NULL |
| 17 | Expand at plan time only what is knowable then |
| 18 | Batches narrow the PK by replacing the temp table's contents |
| 19 | Select batches from the Projects copy, on one code path |
| 20 | Verify PK uniqueness before any batch |
| 21 | Drop and create once per session; runs append |
| 22 | Only the final insert is in a transaction |
| 23 | A failed run does not stop its siblings; a failed phase does |
| 24 | Default resume replays the whole session (amended by D46) |
| 25 | Restore the PK by re-uploading it (amended by D46) |
| 26 | The data dictionary is the source of truth for types |
| 27 | An unknown table is a hard error |

| 29 | Row limits apply to the root PK only |

| 32 | Telemetry has a declared shape |

| 35 | No credentials, and no `.env` required |

| 45 | An unbound table input is an error that suggests, never picks |

| 52 | Retry a failed batch alone, using a `_batch` column |

**The keys research, in brief.** The brief (138 lines) asked the VM's AI three
questions: are keys declared where SQL can read them (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA`,
`sys.foreign_keys`, `sys.indexes`, after a `HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME` probe); do they
hold in the data (`PatientDim.DurableKey` unique with and without
`IsCurrent = 1`, `DiagnosisKey` repeating in `DiagnosisTerminologyDim`,
orphaned diagnosis events); and what does the interactive dictionary show. It
also carried the D50 global-temp probe and the D51 `create_date` query. The
answer (704 lines, transcribed from six screenshots of 11 printed pages) ran
none of the queries. It said keys are hidden from analyst logins rather than
absent; the dictionary cannot be exported, only supplied by Epic; `-1` marks
unmapped or mixture keys and fact tables hold negative placeholder rows;
`DiagnosisTerminologyDim` needs a `Type` filter; `create_date` is not a load
date. It then repeated one uniqueness query and one orphan query for every
key family (patient, encounter, diagnosis, procedure, medication, lab), and
admitted its dictionary descriptions were "paraphrased based on Epic's
conventions, not exact text". What remains useful went into design.md (the
findings with how sure each is, and how to read the `DiagnosisEventFact`
dictionary page, which is kept) and the roadmap (four query shapes, and the
rule that each relationship is graded seen, counted or said, with only the
first two trusted). Both files are in git history before `d6f2030`.

## 11. Open Questions For You

Answer these before anything here becomes a resume line.

1. **The pain point**, in your words. How were Cosmos pulls done before Gen1,
   and how long did one take before and after?
2. **Gen1.** When did it start, how long did it take, how many pulls or
   projects did it serve, and who used its outputs? (The VM brief asks the
   VM's AI for the dates and history.)
3. **Learning.** When did you start SQL, Python and R, and how did you learn
   them?
4. **Tools on 18 to 21 Sep.** Which AI assistant built that work? Those
   commits carry no AI trailer.
5. **The data dictionary.** How were its 2,792 lines built: transcribed from
   the interactive dictionary, with the VM's AI, or by hand?
6. **Transfer mechanics.** How exactly does text get onto the VM, and how do
   screenshots get off it? This is part of the story.
7. **Hand-written work.** Which code or SQL did you write yourself? Be
   precise: interviewers will ask.
8. **Outcomes.** The first live run's results (runtime, whether counts
   matched), time saved per pull, and anyone else who uses or will use
   Telescope.
9. **What can be named.** Your institution, your title, your approvals, and
   whether conversations with Epic can be mentioned.
10. **Git identities.** Are `jungleJM` and `gitea_admin` both you, on
    different machines?
11. **Clinical context.** The research question behind IBD Ancestry, and
    whether it can be described publicly.

**On attribution.** The record shows you made the product, design and
architecture decisions and did all testing on the VM. It also shows that from
22 September most implementation was typed by an AI assistant under your
direction. For a Chief Medical Informatics Officer or Head of Medical
Informatics role, "specified, supervised, tested and shipped, using AI coding
agents" is accurate and is the modern form of managing a development team.
Say it plainly rather than implying you hand-wrote 18,000 lines.
